CCR Improvement Loop — how it works

A ground-up walkthrough: from a repo's merged pull requests to a few defensible numbers and human-approved review-rule proposals.

The one-sentence version. Each run mines a settled window of merged PRs, splits the work so that scripts produce reproducible facts and an LLM agent supplies judgment, and emits a run-*.json of trend metrics plus proposed instruction-file rules — never touching the target repo except through one tracking issue.

1 · The question it answers

Is Copilot Code Review actually helping this repo?

Not "does CCR post comments" — whether those comments reduce human review work, get acted on, and catch what humans catch.

Turning that vague question into numbers is easy to do badly. The tempting shortcuts — line-range overlap to say "CCR caught the same thing", "a later commit touched the file" to say "the comment was addressed", regex sentiment on replies — are all noisy proxies, and no downstream schema rigor fixes a bad proxy.

So the design is deliberately subtractive: a few numbers we can defend, each derived from either a deterministic fact or an explicit LLM judgment over the real diff, never from co-location or keyword guessing. Better three honest numbers than a dozen that look rigorous and rest on sand.

Two more systems wrap this single run: the pacer dispatches many windows over time without blowing the API budget (§9), and the dashboard aggregates every window's run-*.json into trend charts (§10).

3 · Why three phases

Deterministic prep → agent judgment → deterministic math

The split is the core architectural decision (D2). It exists so the agent only ever does the one thing it's uniquely good at — judgment — and everything reproducible stays in code.

Phase Runs as Does Why here
1 · Prep workflow steps (normal network, GITHUB_TOKEN) Fetch settled PRs, deterministically classify & filter, attribute each comment to CCR vs. human, assemble bounded evidence, audit integrity. Facts that must be identical every run: no model, no variance. Produces the normalized cache the agent reads.
2 · Judge the agent job (Copilot engine) Type the PRs rules couldn't; judge each comment against the actual diff; cluster gaps into themes; then call the emit script. Only judgment — "is this ask substantive?", "did they address it?" — needs a model. Bounded, pre-assembled evidence only (D3).
3 · Math emit-run-json.ts + post-steps Compute every rate from the judged rows; validate labels against a closed schema; classify the run's terminal outcome. Arithmetic is deterministic. A hallucinated label is rejected at emit, so it fails the run instead of skewing a metric.
The invariant: scripts produce reproducible facts; the agent supplies judgment. Every number's provenance is one or the other — you can always point at which.

4 · Phase 1 — deterministic prep

P1 Resolve the window identity

Everything keys off a single canonical windowId — resolved before anything is fetched.

resolve-window.ts is a pure function of (repo, window_start, window_end, max_prs, raw-schema). On the weekly schedule it computes a rolling settled window (end = today − 14d, start = end − 14d); a backfill passes the dates explicitly. A scheduled run, a manual dispatch, and a pacer call over the same cohort all resolve to one identical windowId — which is also the cache key, so prep and the cache can never disagree.

Settle lag. We only read PRs merged at least windowLagDays (14) ago, so threads are resolved and follow-up commits have landed before we judge anything.

P1 Fetch → classify → filter → attribute

prep-run.ts orchestrates the stages with explicit-arg subprocess calls, then writes a summary and audits it.

  • Fetch (fetch-prs.ts / pr-graphql.ts) — list every PR merged:>=start merged:<=end and pull its reviews, review comments, and diff hunks. GraphQL is used to tap a separate point budget and cut REST pressure. The raw result is cached as pr-*.json.
  • Classify (classify-pr.ts) — type each PR (bug-fix · feature · refactor · docs · test · chore) only when a label, Conventional-Commit prefix, or linked issue makes it unambiguous. Everything else is left prType: null · needs-agent for Phase 2.
  • Filter (filter-comments.ts) — drop excludedPaths (lockfiles, generated, vendored, minified) so the judge never spends a call on noise.
  • Attribute (attribute-comments.ts) — deterministically split every comment into CCR (from the configured bot logins) vs. human vs. automation. This is a fact, not a guess.
  • Build evidence (build-judge-input.ts) — assemble the bounded evidence the agent may see: each comment plus the line-level diff of what changed after it, and any author replies. Never full files, never excluded paths.
  • Audit — prep-summary.ts writes counts by author kind and identity-integrity checks; prep exits non-zero on a fatal check (e.g. duplicate row ids), failing loudly rather than feeding the agent bad data.

Output: a normalized cache — classified.json, filtered.json, attributed.json, judge-input.json, meta.json, prep-summary.json — that the agent reads but the raw pr-*.json stays the only thing cached across runs (judged artifacts are cheap to recompute; coupling invites staleness, D12).

Why cache only the raw PRs, keyed by windowId + a completion key?

The pr-*.json raw fetch is the expensive part and is immutable for a settled window, so re-dispatching a window is free — the pacer relies on this for zero-rework retries. It's saved only after a successful full fetch under a unique run_id + attempt key, so a half-finished fetch can never poison a later retry. Judged/emitted artifacts are never cached: they recompute in seconds and stale coupling is a bug factory.

5 · Phase 2 — agent judgment

P2 Four jobs, closed vocabulary

The agent works only from judge-input.json's bounded evidence, and every label it may emit comes from a frozen controlled vocabulary.

  1. Classify the leftovers. For every needs-agent PR, pick exactly one prType from the title/labels — so bugFixPrRate reflects the real bug-fix count, not just the machine-typeable subset.
  2. Judge the comments. For each human ask: isSubstantive, diffDetectable, category, and — against that PR's CCR comments — ccrAddressedConcern. For each CCR comment: severity, category, and an outcome of addressed / rejected / ignored / unclear read from the change at those lines plus replies. Results land in judged.json.
  3. Cluster themes. The strict, twice-gated miss flag isGap = ask && isSubstantive && diffDetectable && ccrSawCode && !ccrAddressedConcern is clustered into recurring themes (themes.json) that drive the rule proposals.
  4. Emit & report. Call the deterministic emit script (next section), then route both writes through safe outputs.
There is deliberately no judge.ts model client. The agentic workflow already has model access, so judging in-loop costs zero client code (no endpoint/auth/retry/parsing to rot). What protects the numbers isn't the call mechanism — it's the closed vocabulary enforced at emit: an invalid severity/category/outcome is rejected by the schema, so a hallucinated label fails the run instead of silently skewing a metric.

P3 Compute metrics — the system of record

emit-run-json.ts takes the judged rows and computes every rate deterministically, validating each label through a zod schema before writing: 

node scripts/emit-run-json.ts \
  --meta       $CCR_CACHE/meta.json \
  --classified $CCR_CACHE/classified.json \
  --attributed $CCR_CACHE/judged.json \
  --themes     $CCR_CACHE/themes.json \
  --glob       "$CCR_CACHE/pr-*.json" \
  --out-dir    $CCR_RUNS --print-summary

The resulting run-*.json is the durable record every downstream consumer (the dashboard, the pacer's outcome check) reads. Its schema records the instrument too — judge model, pinned prompt hashes, vocabulary hash — so a trend line can never silently mix two different rulers.

6 · The metrics

Five headline numbers, grouped by question

Each is tagged by provenance: deterministic or LLM-judged.

Q1 — Are humans doing less review work?

humanReviewBurden judged

Are reviewers carrying less?

Average distinct, substantive human asks per PR, sliced by PR type. Counts only asks the judge marked substantive (no LGTM/nit noise) and de-dupes by finding, so chatty threads can't inflate it. Read the trend within one repo — reviewer culture confounds the absolute value.

Q2 — Are CCR's comments useful?

addressedRate / rejectedRate / ignoredRate judged

Do people act on what CCR says? — by severity

For each CCR comment the judge assigns one outcome from a closed set (addressed / rejected / ignored / unclear) read from the actual change at the commented lines plus replies. The three headline rates are the mutually-exclusive shares, sliced by severity — a high ignoredRate on critical comments is a real problem a single "useful rate" would hide. unclear abstains from the denominator.

Q3 — Is CCR catching what humans catch?

ccrRecallRate judged

Of issues humans caught, how many did CCR catch?

Of the substantive, diff-detectable issues human reviewers raised on PRs CCR reviewed, the fraction where CCR independently raised the same concern — an LLM judgment (ccrAddressedConcern), not line-range proximity. Scoped to locally-detectable issues, because the judge sees a truncated hunk; that framing is stated, not hidden.

ccrCoverage deterministic

What share of eligible PRs did CCR review?

Pure fact from review attribution: eligible (post-enablement, non-bot) PRs that got any CCR review. It frames every other Q3 number — a great recall on 30% coverage is a different story than on 95%. Never read alone.

Q4 — Merged-bug signal

bugFixPrRate proxy

Is the merged-bug rate trending?

Share of PRs classified bug-fix. Labeled a proxy, not proof — it counts merged bugs but doesn't attribute them to a review CCR could have caught (causal git blame tracing was tried and removed as too fragile). Watch it alongside recall, never as a headline.

prCycleTime and iterationsPerPr are kept as contextual, low-confidence corroboration only — noisy and multiply-confounded; if they disagree with the burden metric, believe the burden metric.

The five reading rules

These make the difference between a number that means something and one that doesn't. They apply to every metric above.

Trend, not snapshot One window is a data point; a week's PR mix is noise. Read across runs.
n ≥ 5 or suppressed Any figure or slice under 5 is low-confidence and never headlined.
Normalized & sliced Every rate carries prType slices (and severity where it applies), so a heavier bug-fix week can't masquerade as a real move.
Null, never zero "Couldn't measure it" and "it was zero" are different facts, reported differently.
Stable instrument Model + prompt + vocabulary hashes are recorded per run; a shift breaks comparability by design.

7 · The two eligibility guards

Why we don't just say "a human commented, so CCR missed it"

That inference is only ever made under two guards — and getting the first one wrong is what sank the previous design.

  • Same concern, not same line (ccrAddressedConcern). Whether CCR "also caught it" is an LLM judgment that a CCR comment addresses the same concern as the human ask — not overlap of line ranges. Overlap counted two unrelated comments three lines apart as a catch, and missed CCR flagging the same issue class at a different location. Undecidable asks abstain from the denominator.
  • PR-level review gate (ccrReviewed). An ask only enters the recall denominator if CCR reviewed the PR at all.
The cautionary tale: the retired missRate. It used a per-comment ccrSawCode commit-timing gate that flipped to false exactly when a fix commit landed after CCR's review — i.e. precisely when CCR had succeeded. That self-excluded every CCR success and pinned missRate at 1.0 in every run. It was replaced by the PR-level-gated ccrRecallRate (D14). The strict twice-gated isGap flag survives, but only internally to drive theme clustering — never as a headline rate.

8 · Phase 3 — terminal outcome

P3 A machine-readable completion signal

Runs as post-steps (if: always()), so it fires whether the agent succeeded, no-op'd, or failed.

emit-outcome.ts derives one terminal outcome from observable signals — the settled PR count vs. minPrs (50), whether the agent called noop, whether a run-*.json exists on disk, and the job status — and writes outcome-<windowId>.json. The pacer (§9) consumes this as the window's completion signal; the artifact name is derived from the windowId so it correlates offline without inspecting the payload.

Signal Terminal outcome
Any step failed (job.status != success) failed — retryable
< 50 settled PRs, or agent called noop signal-noop — nothing worth reporting
run-*.json produced success

9 · The pacer — backfill at scale

Draining months of history without tripping the rate limit

One run covers one window. To build a trend over many months and repos you need an orchestrator that self-throttles and never loses work.

ccr-pacer.yml is a hand-written hourly cron over the tested planner pace.ts. It runs no agent. Each tick has three jobs:

job 1
plan
backlog − ledger
assertFittable
admit
→
job 2 · matrix
backfill
uses: loop
.lock.yml
→
job 3 · always()
ledger
reconcile →
state branch
  • plan — fetch the durable ccr-pacer-state branch, derive the pending backlog (generated − ledger − skipped), assert every pending window fits a fresh hour's budget, then admit those that fit this tick — ≤ 1 window/repo, ≤ max_windows_per_tick.
  • backfill — a matrix that uses: the loop's reusable .lock.yml once per admitted window. Per-repo child concurrency plus the ≤1/repo rule keep same-repo work serialized.
  • ledger — download every window's outcome artifact, reconcile (missing artifact ⇒ failed; retry cap hit ⇒ skipped.json), and push the updated records back to the state branch.

The starvation guard — a global config property

Each window has a fixed cost estimate from config (est_rest_calls_per_window = 1200, est_graphql_points_per_window = 2000). Because it's a constant, assertFittable checks it against a fresh full hour's usable budget (pool.limit − safety_margin) on every metered pool: 

fresh-hour usable = pool.limit − safety_margin      (e.g. 5000 − 500 = 4500)
if est_rest (1200)    > usable → throw   ← whole config is unfittable
if est_graphql (2000) > usable → throw   ← fails LOUDLY, nothing dispatched
Why loud, not silent. A window that can never fit would otherwise defer forever — no outcome, never reconciled, an invisible leak. So the pacer fails the whole tick with the offending pool and the fix (lower the estimate, raise the ceiling with a per-repo token, or use finer granularity). A window that fits a fresh hour but not this depleted tick is merely deferred, which is fine.

A separate preflight guard inside the loop (--check-budget, on by default) estimates the concrete run against the live budget and aborts before any fetch or cache write if it wouldn't fit — the child-run backstop to the pacer's admission-time check. And a request limiter is the only guard against GitHub's secondary limits, which no tier relaxes.

10 · The dashboard

Static, zero-backend, manifest-driven

The whole point is a trend, so the UI is built to read many run-*.json files and plot them over time.

Every run's run-*.json is dropped in dashboard/data/. A browser can't list a directory, so gen-manifest.ts writes a manifest.json index; aggregate.mjs folds the runs into series and app.mjs draws the charts — no server, no build step. Points key on windowEnd, so same-day backfills still spread across their real windows. Charts slice by prType, severity, PR size bucket (S/M/L/XL by lines changed), and repo. An unmeasured value renders as a gap, never a zero, and low-confidence points are flagged, not headlined. 

# regenerate the index, then serve
node scripts/gen-manifest.ts --data-dir dashboard/data
python3 -m http.server --directory dashboard

11 · Anti-Goodhart & the output

The loop proposes; a human disposes

Every metric here can be gamed if it becomes a target — the fix for "CCR misses things" must never be "tell humans to comment less." So the loop's output is not a repo edit and not a KPI. It is:

  • One tracking issue per run (via a safe output, closing older ones), containing the sliced headline metrics as a trend, the ranked promoted themes with source-PR citations, and — for each theme — one generalized proposed .github/ instruction rule for human approval.
  • One run-*.json artifact — the durable trend record the dashboard reads.
Proposal-only, by construction. The agent job is read-only; every write is routed through safe outputs. It never edits repository files or opens PRs. The metrics are framed as a diagnostic trend gated on a frozen benchmark — if you find yourself tuning the repo to move a number, that's the smell the design is built to resist.

12 · Check your understanding

Five questions

Pick an answer to reveal why it's right or wrong. Then hit Score.

1. Why is the pipeline split into deterministic prep, agent judgment, and deterministic math?
The split (D2) keeps facts reproducible and confines the model to "was this ask substantive? did they address it?" — judgment. A bad label fails the run at emit rather than skewing a metric.
2. Why was missRate retired in favor of ccrRecallRate?
The commit-timing gate closed precisely when a fix commit landed after CCR's review — i.e. when CCR had succeeded — so it excluded every success. ccrRecallRate uses a PR-level review gate instead (D14).
3. How does the system decide CCR "also caught" a human-raised issue?
Same-concern judgment (ccrAddressedConcern) removes the co-location fallacy in both directions — overlap counted unrelated nearby comments as catches and missed same-issue flags elsewhere.
4. On a fresh-hour budget of 5000 with a 500 safety margin, an estimate of 1200 REST calls per window means the pacer will…
assertFittable compares the fixed estimate to limit − margin. 1200 < 4500, so it fits a fresh hour and is admissible (subject to ≤1/repo and max-windows-per-tick). It would only throw if the estimate exceeded 4500.
5. What is a run's actual output — what does it change?
The agent job is read-only and proposal-only: it proposes generalized rules for human approval and records the trend. Framing it as a diagnostic (not a KPI) is the anti-Goodhart guard.
